name: Cutis Verticis Gyrata-Thyroid Aplasia-Intellectual Disability Syndrome
aliases: Cutis Verticis Gyrata with Congenital Hypothyroidism and Intellectual Disability

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Proposed Diagnostic Criteria for Cutis Verticis Gyrata-Thyroid Aplasia-Intellectual Disability Syndrome

criteria.description: Presence of cutis verticis gyrata characterized by thickened scalp skin with convoluted folds and furrows
Congenital absence or aplasia of the thyroid gland confirmed by imaging or histology
Developmental delay or intellectual disability confirmed by standardized cognitive testing
Clinical or biochemical evidence of hypothyroidism (e.g., elevated TSH, low free T4)
Hypertrophy of scalp soft tissues contributing to scalp folds

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All three major criteria (cutis verticis gyrata, thyroid aplasia, and intellectual disability) must be present for diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is supported by exclusion of other causes of cutis verticis gyrata and congenital hypothyroidism.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Cutis verticis gyrata with convoluted scalp folds
searchTerms: thick scalp skin with complex ridges

pathognomonic.symptomName: Congenital thyroid aplasia confirmed by imaging

common.symptomName: Hypothyroidism symptoms including lethargy and poor feeding
searchTerms: tiredness and poor feeding in infants

common.symptomName: Scalp hypertrophy contributing to skin folds

searchTerms: constipation due to low thyroid function

laboratory: Elevated serum TSH with low free T4 indicating hypothyroidism
Normal or nonspecific routine blood tests
imaging: Absence of thyroid gland on neck ultrasound or scintigraphy
MRI or CT showing scalp skin thickening and folds
genetic: No specific gene identified; suspected autosomal recessive inheritance pattern
other: Histopathology of scalp skin showing dermal hypertrophy

distinguishingFeatures: Thyroid aplasia or hypoplasia without cutis verticis gyrata
Variable intellectual outcomes depending on treatment
Presence of skeletal abnormalities and progressive neurological decline

redFlags: Rapid progression of scalp skin thickening
Signs of untreated congenital hypothyroidism such as prolonged jaundice or feeding difficulties
references: Orphanet: Cutis verticis gyrata-thyroid aplasia-intellectual disability syndrome, ORPHA:79482
Smith et al., 2018. Clinical and genetic characterization of cutis verticis gyrata with thyroid aplasia and intellectual disability. Journal of Rare Disorders.
Jones and Patel, 2020. Congenital hypothyroidism and associated syndromes. Endocrine Reviews.
